readerTitle: What Disney really bought when it bought Pixar
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Disney, Pixar, 2006년 인수) + Iger 회고록 속 일화 (홍콩 디즈니랜드 퍼레이드) + 가상 적용 (식료품 체인의 전문 식품점 인수)
insight: 사람과 일하는 방식을 사는 인수에서 통합 계획의 목적은 흡수가 아니라, 산 것을 깨뜨리지 않고 지키는 것이다.
misconception: 인수하면 회사를 소유하게 되니, 효율을 위해 빨리 우리 방식으로 합치는 것이 맞다.

sources.text: The Walt Disney Company press release, Disney to acquire Pixar (January 24, 2006): all-stock deal of about $7.4 billion, Catmull and Lasseter roles, Jobs joining the board
Iger, R. (2019). The Ride of a Lifetime. Random House. (Hong Kong Disneyland parade story, the decision to buy, the written list of Pixar practices to protect)
Catmull, E. (2014). Creativity, Inc. Random House. (keeping the two studios separate, Braintrust-style reviews at Disney Animation)
News coverage of John Lasseter's departure (2018) and Ed Catmull's retirement (announced 2018), e.g. The New York Times, Variety

factChecks.note: 인수 금액 약 74억 달러(전액 주식), 2006년 1월 발표, 2006년 5월 완료. Disney 보도자료로 확인하세요.
Iger의 CEO 취임(2005년 10월), Eisner 시절 Pixar 배급 계약 갱신 협상 결렬(2004년)을 확인하세요. 카드에는 연도 없이 '이전 CEO 시절'로 적었습니다.
홍콩 디즈니랜드 개장(2005년 9월) 퍼레이드 일화는 Iger 회고록에 나오는 본인 서술입니다. 카드에 'he later wrote'로 일화임을 밝혔습니다.
Steve Jobs가 Pixar의 최대 주주였고 인수 후 Disney의 최대 개인 주주이자 이사가 되었다는 점을 확인하세요.
Iger가 Pixar 문화 중 바꾸지 않을 것들을 문서로 약속했다는 내용은 회고록 기준입니다. 세부 항목은 카드에 적지 않았습니다.
Pixar 캠퍼스 위치(캘리포니아 Emeryville), 두 스튜디오를 분리 운영했다는 점(Creativity, Inc.), Tangled(2010)·Frozen(2013) 개봉 연도를 확인하세요. 흥행 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다.
Lasseter 퇴사(2018년, 직장 내 부적절한 행동 의혹), Catmull 은퇴(2018년 발표, 2019년 은퇴)를 게시 직전에 다시 확인하세요.

cards.title: What Disney really bought when it bought Pixar
body: In 2005, Bob Iger had just become Disney's CEO. He later wrote about watching a parade at the opening of Hong Kong Disneyland and noticing something uncomfortable.
Almost every character created in the past decade came from Pixar, a partner studio. Very few came from Disney's own animators.

image.label: A parade float of cartoon characters seen from the crowd
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 테마파크 퍼레이드를 관중 뒤에서 바라본 장면. 앞쪽에 정장 입은 남성의 뒷모습(얼굴 없음). 퍼레이드 캐릭터는 실제 디즈니·픽사 캐릭터가 아닌 오리지널 생물들로. 실제 로고, 캐릭터, 성 모양 상징물은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your partner makes the hits. The deal is ending.
body: Pixar had made its films with Disney since the 1990s, with Disney handling distribution. Under the previous CEO, talks to renew that deal broke down. Meanwhile, Disney's own animation studio had released a run of disappointing films.
You're Iger. What do you do?

options.text: Rebuild Disney's own studio: hire, invest and give it time
options.feedback: You keep full control and spend less cash. But it could take years, and this studio already had money and talent and still struggled.

options.text: Win back the partnership by offering Pixar better terms
options.feedback: The films keep coming without a huge price tag. But Pixar keeps more of the upside, and you face another standoff at the next renewal.

options.text: Buy Pixar outright, even at a very high price
options.feedback: You secure the studio and its future films. But you pay a large premium and risk breaking the very thing you bought.

cards.title: About $7.4 billion for a handful of films.
body: Iger chose to buy. In January 2006, Disney announced the deal: about **$7.4 billion**, paid in Disney stock. Steve Jobs, Pixar's largest shareholder, became Disney's largest individual shareholder and joined its board.
Pixar had released only a handful of feature films. Even great films don't explain that price. Disney was paying for what *made* those films: Pixar's people and its way of working.

cards.title: Buying a capability
body: A **capability** is a business's repeatable way of producing results: its people, habits and methods working together.

A factory or a film library stays put after a sale. A capability doesn't. If key people leave, or their habits get crushed under the buyer's rules, the thing you paid for disappears, even though the paperwork says you own it.
The same is true when an accounting firm buys a smaller one for its partners' client relationships.

image.label: A building that stays put next to people walking out a door
image.brief: 좌우 2분할 인포그래픽. 왼쪽: 'Assets' 라벨과 함께 공장·필름 릴 아이콘이 자물쇠로 고정됨. 오른쪽: 'Capability' 라벨과 함께 사람 세 명이 문 밖으로 걸어 나가는 모습, 점선 화살표. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.softwareNote: Software companies often buy small startups mainly for their engineers, sometimes called an *acqui-hire*. If those engineers leave once their retention bonuses pay out, the buyer is left with code nobody understands.

cards.title: Disney built the merger around not breaking Pixar.
body: Iger later wrote that he agreed in writing to a list of Pixar practices Disney would not change. The structure followed the same logic:
list: **Pixar kept** its name and its own campus in Emeryville, California
**Ed Catmull and John Lasseter**, Pixar's leaders, were put in charge of Disney's own animation studio too
**The two studios stayed separate**, rather than being merged into one
cards.callout: The buyer put the bought company's leaders in charge of its own struggling unit, not the other way around.

cards.title: The real gain showed up at the other studio.
body: Pixar kept making films, including *Up* and *Toy Story 3*.

The bigger surprise was Disney Animation. Under Catmull and Lasseter, it took on Pixar-style habits, such as frank peer reviews of films while they were still rough. It went on to make hits like *Tangled* (2010) and *Frozen* (2013).
Disney didn't just gain Pixar's films. It spread Pixar's **way of working** to a second studio.

image.label: Two separate studio buildings linked by a path of shared notes
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 서로 다른 모양의 스튜디오 건물 두 채가 떨어져 서 있고, 그 사이를 스토리보드 메모지들이 길처럼 이어줌. 두 건물은 합쳐지지 않음. 실제 로고, 캐릭터, 건물 외관은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A capability that lives in a few people is fragile.
body: In 2018, Lasseter left the company after allegations of workplace misconduct, and Catmull announced his retirement soon after. When a capability depends on a few leaders, it can weaken when they go.
Fit with the buyer matters too. Disney could carry Pixar's characters into parks, toys and TV. A buyer without that reach might not have been able to justify the same price.

cards.title: Now it's a grocery chain.
body: You run a regional grocery chain with 60 stores. You're buying a 12-store specialty food shop known for its buyers, who find small local producers, and staff who can talk customers through every cheese.
Your goal is to make your own stores better at fresh and specialty food. How do you integrate?

options.text: Move them onto your central buying and shelf plans within 90 days to cut costs
options.feedback: You get quick savings on purchasing. But central buying replaces the very buyers and local producers you paid for, and the best staff may leave.

options.text: Keep their name, buyers and store practices, and put their head buyer in charge of specialty food across all your stores
options.feedback: You protect what made them special and spread it to your 60 stores, like Disney did with its animation studio. The cost is slower savings and two ways of working side by side.

options.text: Leave them completely alone as a separate business
options.feedback: The capability survives, but your own stores learn nothing from it. You paid a premium for skills that never reach your main business.

cards.title: When you buy how a business works, protect it first.
body: Before buying a company, name what you're actually paying for. If it's people and their way of working, build the integration plan to keep it alive, then spread it.
**Try it today:** pick a team, supplier or partner you rely on. Write down what makes them good. Then list which of your own rules would break it if they joined you.
